category: Tcl Environment, Vitis HLS, Vitis & Vivado GUI
description: The Tcl interpreter and property system that every other Vivado command is built on, the Vitis HLS flow that compiles C/C++ into RTL, the Vitis and XSCT tools that take a bitstream to a running board, and the GUI windows that all of it maps onto.

tools.name: source
tools.description: Read and execute a Tcl script in the current Vivado session. It is how a build is broken into reusable pieces - a part definition, a constraints helper, a library of procedures - and how a script generated by write_project_tcl or write_bd_tcl is replayed. By default every command in the sourced file is echoed to the console and the journal, which -notrace suppresses.

parameters.name: <filename>
parameters.description: Path to the Tcl file. Relative paths resolve against the current working directory, not the script's own directory, which is the usual source of 'file not found' in a sourced script.

parameters.name: -notrace
parameters.description: Do not echo each command as it executes. Keeps the log readable when sourcing a long generated script.

parameters.name: -quiet
parameters.description: Suppress the error and return an empty result if the file cannot be read, instead of aborting the script.

parameters.name: -verbose
parameters.description: Emit extra informational messages about what is being sourced.

tools.example:
# Split a build into reusable pieces
source -notrace ./tcl/settings.tcl
source -notrace ./tcl/read_sources.tcl
source -notrace ./tcl/build_bd.tcl

# Make paths relative to the script itself rather than the cwd
set here [file dirname [file normalize [info script]]]
source -notrace [file join $here helpers.tcl]

# Replay a project rebuild script emitted earlier
source -notrace ./rebuild_project.tcl
tools.notes: Use `[file dirname [file normalize [info script]]]` to anchor paths to the script rather than the launch directory; this is the single most common portability bug in Vivado build scripts. `vivado -mode batch -source` is the equivalent from the command line.

tools.name: vivado -mode batch -source
tools.description: The headless entry point: launch Vivado, run a Tcl script and exit. This is what a CI job or a Makefile calls. Script arguments are passed after -tclargs and arrive in the standard Tcl variables $argc and $argv, so one build script can serve several parts, top modules or output directories.

parameters.name: -mode
parameters.description: batch runs the script and exits; tcl gives an interactive shell with no GUI; gui launches the interface, optionally sourcing a script first.

parameters.name: -source
parameters.description: The Tcl script to execute.

parameters.name: -tclargs
parameters.description: Everything after this switch is handed to the script as $argv, with $argc holding the count. It must be the last switch on the command line.

parameters.name: -log / -journal
parameters.description: Rename vivado.log and vivado.jou. Essential when several jobs run in one directory, because they otherwise collide.

parameters.name: -nolog / -nojournal
parameters.description: Suppress the log or journal entirely.

parameters.name: -notrace
parameters.description: Do not echo each sourced command.

parameters.name: -tempDir
parameters.description: Redirect Vivado's temporary files, useful on build machines with a small system drive.

tools.example:
# build.tcl
if {$argc < 2} { error "usage: build.tcl <part> <top>" }
set part [lindex $argv 0]
set top  [lindex $argv 1]
create_project -in_memory -part $part
read_verilog [glob ./src/*.v]
read_xdc ./constrs/top.xdc
synth_design -top $top -part $part
opt_design
place_design
route_design
report_timing_summary -file ./reports/timing.rpt
write_bitstream -force ./out/${top}.bit

# Shell
vivado -mode batch -source build.tcl \
  -log build.log -journal build.jou -notrace \
  -tclargs xcku040-ffva1156-2-e top
tools.notes: Vivado returns a non-zero exit status when the script raises an error, so a CI job can gate on it - but only if the script actually uses `error` rather than printing a message. Wrap the flow in a catch and re-raise, or check WNS explicitly, so a timing failure fails the build.

tools.name: get_property
tools.description: Read the value of a property from any first-class Vivado object: a cell, net, port, clock, run, fileset, IP, hardware device or the project itself. Together with set_property it is the uniform accessor that replaces dozens of special-purpose query commands, and it is how a script inspects run status, part details, file types and timing results.

parameters.name: <property_name>
parameters.description: Property to read, case-insensitive, e.g. STATUS, PROGRESS, SLACK, FILE_TYPE, PART, TOP, NAME.

parameters.name: <object>
parameters.description: A single object, normally the result of a get_* command. Passing a list of several objects is an error; iterate instead.

parameters.name: -min / -max
parameters.description: For properties that carry separate minimum and maximum values, such as delay-related properties on timing objects.

parameters.name: -quiet
parameters.description: Return an empty string rather than erroring when the property does not exist on that object class.

tools.example:
# Poll a run and fail the build if it did not finish
launch_runs impl_1 -to_step write_bitstream -jobs 8
wait_on_run impl_1
set st [get_property STATUS   [get_runs impl_1]]
set pr [get_property PROGRESS [get_runs impl_1]]
if {$pr ne "100%"} { error "impl_1 did not complete: $st" }

# Gate on timing
set wns [get_property SLACK [get_timing_paths -delay_type max]]
puts "WNS = $wns ns"

# Inspect the design
puts "part: [get_property PART [current_project]]"
puts "top:  [get_property TOP  [current_fileset]]"
tools.notes: PROGRESS is the string "100%", not the number 100, so compare it as a string. Use report_property to see every property an object carries and list_property to enumerate names programmatically.

tools.name: set_property
tools.description: Write a property onto one or more design, project or run objects. It is the single most-used command in Vivado scripting: constraints, run strategies, synthesis options, file types, IP configuration and bitstream settings are all expressed as properties. The -dict form sets several properties in one call, which is both faster and much more readable.

parameters.name: <property_name> <value>
parameters.description: The property and the value to assign. Names are case-insensitive; values are validated against the property's legal set.

parameters.name: -dict
parameters.description: A flat {name value name value ...} list applied to the same object(s) in one call. Preferred whenever more than one property is being set.

parameters.name: <objects>
parameters.description: One object or a collection from a get_* command. Unlike get_property, set_property happily accepts a whole collection.

parameters.name: -quiet
parameters.description: Suppress the error when the property or object does not exist.

tools.example:
# Project and run configuration
set_property top top [current_fileset]
set_property board_part xilinx.com:zcu104:part0:1.1 [current_project]
set_property STEPS.SYNTH_DESIGN.ARGS.FLATTEN_HIERARCHY rebuilt [get_runs synth_1]
set_property strategy Performance_Explore [get_runs impl_1]

# Several properties in one call
set_property -dict {
  PACKAGE_PIN AH11
  IOSTANDARD  DIFF_SSTL12
} [get_ports sys_clk_p]

# Applied across a collection
set_property ASYNC_REG TRUE [get_cells -hier -filter {NAME =~ *sync_ff_reg[*]}]
tools.notes: An invalid value produces an error naming the legal set; list_property_value shows that set in advance. Properties set on a run only take effect on the next launch_runs, not on a run already in progress.

tools.name: report_property
tools.description: Print every property of an object with its type, whether it is read-only, and its current value. It is the discovery command for the whole property system: when you do not know what can be queried or set on a run, a cell, an IP or a hardware device, this is how you find out without leaving the tool.

parameters.name: <object>
parameters.description: The object to inspect, from any get_* command.

parameters.name: <pattern>
parameters.description: Restrict the listing to property names matching a glob pattern, e.g. STEPS.* or BITSTREAM.*.

parameters.name: -all
parameters.description: Include properties that are not currently set, so the full available set is shown.

parameters.name: -class
parameters.description: Report the properties of an object class by name rather than of a specific instance.

parameters.name: -regexp
parameters.description: Treat the pattern as a regular expression.

parameters.name: -file / -return_string
parameters.description: Write the report to a file or return it as a Tcl string for parsing.

tools.example:
# What can I set on an implementation run?
report_property -all [get_runs impl_1] STEPS.*

# What does this IP expose?
report_property [get_ips axi_gpio_0] CONFIG.*

# Every bitstream option valid for this part
report_property -all [current_design] BITSTREAM.*

# Class-level discovery without an instance
report_property -class run -all
tools.notes: report_property prints for humans; list_property returns a Tcl list for scripting. Together they are the fastest route to any Vivado capability that is not already documented in a build script you have.

tools.name: list_property
tools.description: Return the names of the properties available on an object or object class as a Tcl list, so a script can iterate over them. Its companion list_property_value returns the legal values of one property, which is how you discover the valid strategies, directives or file types for the release you are running rather than hard-coding a list that changes between versions.

parameters.name: <object>
parameters.description: Object whose property names are listed.

parameters.name: <pattern>
parameters.description: Glob pattern restricting the names returned.

parameters.name: -class
parameters.description: List the properties of a class (run, cell, net, port, fileset, ip, ...) without needing an instance.

parameters.name: list_property_value <name> <object>
parameters.description: Return the legal values of one enumerated property on that object.

parameters.name: -default
parameters.description: For list_property_value, return the default value rather than the full set.

tools.example:
# Which implementation strategies does this release offer?
puts [list_property_value strategy [get_runs impl_1]]

# Which synthesis step arguments exist?
foreach p [list_property [get_runs synth_1] STEPS.SYNTH_DESIGN.ARGS.*] {
  puts [format "%-55s = %s" $p [get_property $p [get_runs synth_1]]]
}

# Legal file types
puts [list_property_value FILE_TYPE [lindex [get_files] 0]]
tools.notes: Directive and strategy names change between Vivado releases, so a script that discovers them with list_property_value survives an upgrade where a hard-coded string does not.

tools.name: set_param
tools.description: Set an internal Vivado configuration parameter for the current session, controlling behaviour that is not exposed as an object property: thread counts, message limits, DRC waivers, IP cache behaviour and various tool-specific switches. get_param reads one back and report_params lists them. Parameters are session-scoped, so they belong at the top of a build script.

parameters.name: general.maxThreads
parameters.description: Maximum number of threads any single sub-process may use. Raising it speeds up synthesis and routing on a large machine.

parameters.name: messaging.defaultLimit
parameters.description: How many times a repeated message is printed before being suppressed; raise it when a warning is being truncated before you can read it all.

parameters.name: project.enableIPCacheLiteLoad
parameters.description: Controls out-of-context IP cache behaviour, which affects incremental rebuild times on IP-heavy projects.

parameters.name: get_param
parameters.description: Read the current value of a parameter.

parameters.name: report_params
parameters.description: List parameters whose value differs from the default, which is the practical way to see what a script has changed.

tools.example:
set_param general.maxThreads 8
set_param messaging.defaultLimit 10000
puts "maxThreads = [get_param general.maxThreads]"

# Record what this script changed, for the build log
report_params -file ./reports/params.rpt
tools.notes: Parameters are undocumented tuning knobs in many cases and some are release-specific; report_params is the safe way to see what exists in your install. They do not persist between sessions, so set them in the build script rather than relying on a saved preference.

tools.name: help
tools.description: Print the syntax, argument list and description of a Vivado Tcl command from inside the tool, or list the commands in a category. Because it reflects the exact release you are running, it is more reliable than any external reference for checking whether a switch exists. Every command also accepts -help for the same information.

parameters.name: <command_name>
parameters.description: Print full help for one command, including every switch and its meaning.

parameters.name: -category
parameters.description: List the commands in a category such as Project, Design Analysis, XDC, IPIntegrator, Hardware, SimulationBuild.

parameters.name: -args
parameters.description: Print only the argument summary rather than the full description.

parameters.name: <command> -help
parameters.description: Equivalent per-command form, convenient while composing a command line.

tools.notes: The journal file (vivado.jou) complements this: perform an action in the GUI, then read the journal to see the exact Tcl command and switches Vivado used. Between `help` and the journal, no external documentation is needed to write a build script.

tools.name: start_gui
tools.description: Bring up the graphical interface on top of the design currently in memory, and stop_gui drops back to the shell without losing it. Together they make it practical to run a headless build, stop at a failure, open the GUI to look at the schematic or the failing path interactively, then close it and continue the script.

parameters.name: start_gui
parameters.description: Launch the interface on the current in-memory project or checkpoint. Works from `vivado -mode tcl` and from a paused batch script.

parameters.name: stop_gui
parameters.description: Close the interface and return to the Tcl prompt with the design still loaded.

parameters.name: Requirements
parameters.description: Needs a display (X11 or a Windows desktop); it will fail on a headless build node.

tools.example:
# Interactive triage of a routed checkpoint
vivado -mode tcl
open_checkpoint ./post_route.dcp
report_timing_summary -file ./timing.rpt
start_gui
# ... inspect the failing path in the GUI ...
stop_gui
report_design_analysis -congestion -file ./congestion.rpt
exit
tools.notes: A common debugging pattern is to add `if {$::env(DEBUG) eq "1"} { start_gui }` to a build script so the same script serves CI and interactive use. Do not leave it in a script that runs on a build server, because the GUI will block waiting for a display.

tools.name: vitis_hls
tools.description: The Vitis HLS executable, which compiles C, C++ or OpenCL into RTL. In a build it is called with -f to run a Tcl script headless; -p opens an existing project in the GUI and -i gives an interactive Tcl shell. Releases up to 2020.1 shipped the same tool as vivado_hls with an almost identical command set.

parameters.name: -f
parameters.description: Run a Tcl script headless and exit. The standard batch entry point.

parameters.name: -p
parameters.description: Open an existing project directory in the graphical interface.

parameters.name: -i
parameters.description: Start an interactive Tcl shell with the HLS command set.

parameters.name: -l
parameters.description: Write the session log to a named file instead of vitis_hls.log.

parameters.name: Arguments to the script
parameters.description: Values after the script name are available to it; a common alternative is to read environment variables with $::env(NAME).

tools.example:
# run_hls.tcl
open_project -reset fir_prj
add_files fir.cpp
add_files -tb fir_test.cpp
set_top fir
open_solution -reset "solution1" -flow_target vivado
set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
create_clock -period 3.33 -name default
csim_design
csynth_design
cosim_design -rtl verilog
export_design -format ip_catalog -display_name "FIR Filter"
exit

# Shell
vitis_hls -f run_hls.tcl -l hls_build.log
tools.notes: The script must end with `exit` or the tool stays open waiting for input, which hangs a CI job. Exit status is non-zero when a stage fails, so a build can gate on it directly.

tools.name: open_project
tools.description: Create or open a Vitis HLS project, which is the container for the design sources, the testbench and one or more solutions. The -reset switch deletes any existing project of that name and starts clean, which is what a repeatable build script always wants so that stale results cannot leak between runs.

parameters.name: <project_name>
parameters.description: Project directory name, created relative to the working directory.

parameters.name: -reset
parameters.description: Delete and recreate the project, discarding all previous solutions and results. Use it in every scripted build.

parameters.name: Relationship to solutions
parameters.description: A project holds the sources and top function; each solution under it holds one target part, clock and set of directives.

tools.example:
open_project -reset fir_prj
add_files fir.cpp
add_files -tb fir_test.cpp
set_top fir

# Several solutions explore different targets from one project
foreach {sol period} {solution_fast 3.33 solution_slow 10.0} {
  open_solution -reset $sol -flow_target vivado
  set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
  create_clock -period $period -name default
  csynth_design
}
tools.notes: Without -reset, results from an earlier run remain and a failed synthesis can appear to succeed because the old report is still there. close_project closes it explicitly, though `exit` at the end of a script is usually enough.

tools.name: add_files
tools.description: Add design or testbench sources to a Vitis HLS project. Files added plainly are synthesised; files added with -tb are testbench only and are compiled for C simulation and co-simulation but never turned into RTL. Compiler flags for each group are passed with -cflags, which is how include paths and standards are set.

parameters.name: <files>
parameters.description: One or more source files; a Tcl list or glob works.

parameters.name: -tb
parameters.description: Mark the files as testbench. They are excluded from synthesis and their data files travel with them.

parameters.name: -cflags
parameters.description: Flags passed to the compiler for these files, e.g. "-I./inc -std=c++14 -DFIXED_POINT".

parameters.name: -csimflags
parameters.description: Extra flags used only during C simulation, such as -g for debug symbols.

parameters.name: -blackbox
parameters.description: Supply a JSON description so an existing RTL block is instantiated instead of being synthesised from C.

tools.example:
open_project -reset fir_prj
add_files fir.cpp -cflags "-I./inc -std=c++14"
add_files -tb fir_test.cpp -cflags "-I./inc -std=c++14"
add_files -tb ./data/golden.dat
set_top fir

# Several design files at once
add_files [glob ./src/*.cpp] -cflags "-I./inc"
tools.notes: The -cflags must usually match between the design and testbench groups, or C simulation compiles headers differently from synthesis and the two disagree. Data files consumed by the testbench must be added with -tb so they are copied into the simulation directory.

tools.name: set_top
tools.description: Name the C or C++ function that becomes the top level of the generated RTL. Everything reachable from it is synthesised into the block; everything else is testbench. The function's arguments become the RTL ports, so the choice of top function is also the choice of interface.

parameters.name: <function_name>
parameters.description: Name of the top function. For an overloaded or templated C++ function, the name may need the fully resolved form, and a simple extern "C" wrapper is often the practical answer.

parameters.name: Effect on interfaces
parameters.description: Each top-level argument is mapped to an RTL interface, controlled by #pragma HLS INTERFACE.

parameters.name: Ordering
parameters.description: Must be called after add_files and before csynth_design.

tools.notes: If synthesis reports that the top function cannot be found, the usual causes are C++ name mangling on an overloaded function or a typo in the name; wrapping the call in an extern "C" function removes the ambiguity.

tools.name: open_solution
tools.description: Create or open a solution inside the current project. A solution is one attempt at implementing the design: it owns the target part, the clock, the flow target and the directives, so several solutions let you compare micro-architectures side by side in the GUI's comparison view without touching the source.

parameters.name: <solution_name>
parameters.description: Solution directory name inside the project.

parameters.name: -reset
parameters.description: Discard any existing solution of that name and its results. Use it in scripted builds.

parameters.name: -flow_target vivado
parameters.description: Target the Vivado IP flow, producing an IP for the IP catalog or a block design.

parameters.name: -flow_target vitis
parameters.description: Target the Vitis acceleration flow, producing a .xo kernel with the interfaces that flow expects.

tools.example:
open_project -reset fir_prj
add_files fir.cpp
add_files -tb fir_test.cpp
set_top fir

# Compare two micro-architectures
open_solution -reset "sol_pipelined" -flow_target vivado
set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
create_clock -period 3.33 -name default
csynth_design

open_solution -reset "sol_dataflow" -flow_target vivado
set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
create_clock -period 3.33 -name default
csynth_design
tools.notes: The flow target changes the default interface synthesis: a vitis-target solution assumes AXI master and s_axilite control, a vivado-target one leaves more control to the INTERFACE pragmas. Choosing the wrong one produces a block that will not connect in the intended flow.

tools.name: set_part
tools.description: Choose the target device for the current solution, which determines the available resources and the timing characterisation used for scheduling. Changing the part changes the achievable clock and therefore the whole schedule, so it must be set before csynth_design and is a property of the solution rather than the project.

parameters.name: <part_name>
parameters.description: Full device string, e.g. {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e} or {xczu7ev-ffvc1156-2-e}. Braces protect the hyphens from Tcl.

parameters.name: <board_part>
parameters.description: A board identifier can be used instead of a raw part when a board file is installed.

parameters.name: Scope
parameters.description: Applies to the currently open solution only, so different solutions can target different devices.

parameters.name: Ordering
parameters.description: Set it after open_solution and before create_clock and csynth_design.

tools.example:
open_solution -reset "solution1" -flow_target vivado
set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
create_clock -period 3.33 -name default
csynth_design

# Sweep the target device from one script
foreach part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e xczu7ev-ffvc1156-2-e} {
  open_solution -reset "sol_$part" -flow_target vivado
  set_part $part
  create_clock -period 5 -name default
  csynth_design
}
tools.notes: Always brace the part string: without braces Tcl leaves it intact here, but the habit matters in the many places where a bracketed or hyphenated argument would otherwise be reinterpreted. An unavailable part produces an error naming the installed device families.

tools.name: create_clock (Vitis HLS)
tools.description: Set the target clock period that high-level synthesis schedules against, and optionally an uncertainty margin. It is the single most influential control in HLS: the period decides how much logic fits in a cycle, and therefore the pipeline depth, the resource count and whether an initiation interval of 1 is achievable at all. Note this is the HLS command, distinct from the identically named XDC constraint in Vivado.

parameters.name: -period
parameters.description: Target clock period. A bare number is nanoseconds; a unit suffix such as 300MHz is also accepted in recent releases.

parameters.name: -name
parameters.description: Clock name, conventionally `default` for a single-clock design.

parameters.name: set_clock_uncertainty
parameters.description: Margin subtracted from the period before scheduling, reserving room for the downstream place-and-route. Defaults to around 12% of the period; raise it when HLS meets timing but Vivado does not.

parameters.name: Multiple clocks
parameters.description: Additional clocks can be created for designs with more than one clock domain, though most HLS kernels are single-clock.

tools.notes: HLS reports an estimated period that does not include routing delay, so a design that just meets timing in HLS frequently fails in Vivado. Increasing set_clock_uncertainty is the standard remedy, and is cheaper than re-architecting after the fact.

tools.name: csim_design
tools.description: Compile and run the C testbench against the untouched C source, before any synthesis. It is pure software execution, so it is fast, and it verifies the algorithm and the testbench's self-checking logic. A testbench that does not return 0 on success is useless to the rest of the flow, because co-simulation relies on that return value.

parameters.name: -clean
parameters.description: Rebuild the simulation from scratch, discarding previously compiled objects.

parameters.name: -setup
parameters.description: Build the simulation executable but do not run it, so it can be launched under a debugger.

parameters.name: -argv
parameters.description: Command-line arguments passed to the testbench main function, typically data file paths.

parameters.name: -ldflags
parameters.description: Extra linker flags, for example to link a reference library the testbench compares against.

parameters.name: -profile
parameters.description: Collect profiling data to find which functions dominate runtime, which guides where to focus optimisation.

tools.example:
add_files fir.cpp
add_files -tb fir_test.cpp
add_files -tb ./data/input.dat
set_top fir
open_solution -reset "solution1" -flow_target vivado
set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
create_clock -period 3.33 -name default
csim_design -clean -argv "./data/input.dat"
tools.notes: The testbench main must return 0 for pass and non-zero for fail; cosim_design uses exactly that convention to decide whether RTL matches C. A testbench that always returns 0 makes co-simulation pass no matter how wrong the hardware is.

tools.name: csynth_design
tools.description: Run high-level synthesis: schedule the C code into states, bind operations to hardware resources, and generate RTL together with a synthesis report giving estimated timing, latency, initiation interval and resource usage. It is the central step of the flow and the point at which pragmas take effect.

parameters.name: Inputs
parameters.description: The current solution's part, clock, source files, top function and directives.

parameters.name: Outputs
parameters.description: Verilog and VHDL RTL under <solution>/syn, plus the synthesis report under <solution>/syn/report.

parameters.name: Key report figures
parameters.description: Estimated clock period, latency in cycles, initiation interval (II), and BRAM/DSP/FF/LUT counts.

parameters.name: Failure to meet II
parameters.description: Reported as a warning with the limiting dependency named, which is the main diagnostic for pipelining problems.

tools.example:
csynth_design

# Read the key numbers back in a scripted exploration
# (the report is also available as XML under <solution>/syn/report)
puts "synthesis complete - see fir_prj/solution1/syn/report/fir_csynth.rpt"

# Typical exploration loop
foreach ii {1 2 4} {
  open_solution -reset "sol_ii$ii" -flow_target vivado
  set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
  create_clock -period 3.33 -name default
  csynth_design
}
tools.notes: Estimated timing excludes routing delay, so treat the reported period as optimistic and leave margin via set_clock_uncertainty. When II is worse than requested, the report names the carried dependency preventing it - that message is the actual fix, not a directive to add.

tools.name: cosim_design
tools.description: Run C/RTL co-simulation: the same C testbench drives the generated RTL through a simulator, and the pass or fail verdict comes from the testbench's return value. It is the only automatic check that the generated hardware actually matches the C model, and it also measures the real latency and initiation interval rather than the synthesis estimate.

parameters.name: -rtl
parameters.description: Which generated RTL to simulate, verilog or vhdl.

parameters.name: -tool
parameters.description: Simulator to use; xsim ships with the tools and needs no extra licence.

parameters.name: -trace_level
parameters.description: none is fastest; port dumps the top-level interface waveform; all dumps everything and is very slow but shows internal behaviour.

parameters.name: -argv
parameters.description: Arguments passed to the testbench, matching what csim_design used.

parameters.name: -setup
parameters.description: Generate the simulation scripts without running, so the simulator can be driven manually.

tools.example:
csynth_design
cosim_design -rtl verilog -tool xsim -trace_level port -argv "./data/input.dat"

# The waveform lands under:
#   <project>/<solution>/sim/verilog/*.wdb
# and can be opened with:
#   xsim --gui <snapshot>.wdb
tools.notes: Co-simulation is much slower than C simulation, so keep the testbench dataset small - a few hundred samples is usually enough to prove equivalence. A pass here with an incorrect testbench proves nothing, so verify the testbench actually fails when you corrupt the golden data.

tools.name: export_design
tools.description: Package the synthesised RTL for downstream use: as an IP for the Vivado IP catalog, as a .xo kernel object for the Vitis acceleration flow, or as a synthesised design checkpoint. It can optionally run Vivado synthesis or implementation on the block first, which replaces the HLS estimates with real timing and resource numbers.

parameters.name: -format ip_catalog
parameters.description: Produce a packaged IP (a zip) that can be added to a Vivado IP repository and instantiated in a block design.

parameters.name: -format xo
parameters.description: Produce a Vitis kernel object for linking with v++ into an .xclbin.

parameters.name: -flow syn | impl
parameters.description: Run Vivado synthesis or full implementation on the exported block to obtain real timing and utilisation instead of HLS estimates.

parameters.name: -display_name / -description
parameters.description: Metadata shown in the Vivado IP catalog.

parameters.name: -vendor / -library / -version
parameters.description: The VLNV fields of the packaged IP, which determine how it is referenced by create_bd_cell.

parameters.name: -output
parameters.description: Destination path for the generated archive or object.

tools.example:
# IP for a Vivado block design
export_design -format ip_catalog -rtl verilog \
  -vendor "mycompany.com" -library hls -version 1.0 \
  -display_name "FIR Filter" -output ./ip/fir_ip.zip

# Kernel for the Vitis acceleration flow
export_design -format xo -output ./fir.xo

# Get real numbers rather than HLS estimates
export_design -format ip_catalog -flow impl
tools.notes: `-flow impl` takes far longer but is the only way to know whether the block really meets the clock, because HLS estimates exclude routing. In Vivado, add the exported zip's directory to IP_REPO_PATHS and run update_ip_catalog before the IP appears.

tools.name: config_interface
tools.description: Set solution-wide defaults for how top-level arguments become RTL interfaces, so that per-argument INTERFACE pragmas only have to cover the exceptions. The companion config_compile sets global compilation behaviour such as automatic loop pipelining and floating-point optimisation. Both are solution properties, so they belong in the run script rather than the source.

parameters.name: -m_axi_addr64
parameters.description: Use 64-bit addressing on AXI master interfaces, required for platforms with more than 4 GB of addressable memory.

parameters.name: -default_slave_interface
parameters.description: Default control interface for scalar arguments and the block's start/done handshake, normally s_axilite.

parameters.name: -m_axi_offset
parameters.description: Where the AXI master base address comes from: off, direct (a port) or slave (a register in the s_axilite map).

parameters.name: -clock_enable
parameters.description: Add a clock-enable port to the generated block.

parameters.name: config_compile -pipeline_loops
parameters.description: Automatically pipeline loops whose trip count is at or below this threshold, without needing a pragma on each.

parameters.name: config_compile -unsafe_math_optimizations
parameters.description: Allow floating-point reassociation, which reduces latency at the cost of bit-exact reproducibility.

tools.example:
open_solution -reset "solution1" -flow_target vitis
set_part {xcu250-figd2104-2L-e}
create_clock -period 3.33 -name default

config_interface -m_axi_addr64 -m_axi_offset slave -default_slave_interface s_axilite
config_compile -pipeline_loops 64

csynth_design
export_design -format xo -output ./fir.xo
tools.notes: Interface defaults differ between the vivado and vitis flow targets, so a solution that works in one can produce an unconnectable block in the other. Set them explicitly here when the design must build in both.

tools.name: #pragma HLS PIPELINE
tools.description: Pipeline a loop or function so a new input can be accepted every II cycles instead of waiting for the previous iteration to finish. It is the primary throughput directive in HLS and usually the first one applied. The achievable II is limited by loop-carried dependencies and by resource contention, both of which the synthesis report names when the target is missed.

parameters.name: II
parameters.description: Target initiation interval in cycles. II=1 accepts new data every cycle and is the usual goal.

parameters.name: rewind
parameters.description: For a loop inside a function called repeatedly, allow the next invocation to start before the pipeline has fully drained.

parameters.name: off
parameters.description: Explicitly disable pipelining, used to override an enclosing directive or config_compile -pipeline_loops.

parameters.name: style
parameters.description: stp (stall pipeline, the default), flp (flushable) or frp (free-running), trading area against how the pipeline handles stalls.

parameters.name: Placement
parameters.description: Inside a loop body pipelines that loop; at function scope pipelines the whole function and unrolls the loops it contains.

tools.notes: Pipelining a loop automatically unrolls any loops nested inside it, which can be a large and surprising area cost. When II=1 cannot be met, read the report's dependency message rather than adding more directives - the fix is nearly always in the code, such as an array partition or a removed accumulator dependency.

tools.name: #pragma HLS UNROLL
tools.description: Replicate a loop body so several iterations execute in parallel, trading area for latency. A full unroll removes the loop entirely; a partial unroll with factor=N creates N copies and keeps a loop with 1/N the trips. It is essential for small inner loops such as filter taps, and ruinous if applied to a large outer loop.

parameters.name: factor
parameters.description: Number of copies to create. Omitting it unrolls the loop completely, which requires a compile-time-known trip count.

parameters.name: skip_exit_check
parameters.description: Omit the per-copy bounds check when the trip count is known to be an exact multiple of the factor. Produces wrong results if that is not true.

parameters.name: region
parameters.description: Unroll all loops within the enclosing region rather than a single loop.

parameters.name: Interaction with arrays
parameters.description: Unrolling only helps if the array accesses can happen in parallel, which usually needs a matching ARRAY_PARTITION.

tools.notes: Unrolling without partitioning the arrays it reads gives no speedup at all, because a two-port BRAM still allows only two accesses per cycle - the loop simply stalls. Always pair the two directives.

tools.name: #pragma HLS ARRAY_PARTITION
tools.description: Split an array into several smaller memories or into individual registers, so more elements can be read and written in the same cycle. Memory port count is the most common reason a pipelined loop cannot reach II=1, and this directive is the fix. Complete partitioning turns the array into registers, which is fast but expensive for anything large.

parameters.name: variable
parameters.description: The array to partition.

parameters.name: type=complete
parameters.description: Every element becomes its own register. Full parallel access, but the area cost grows with the array size.

parameters.name: type=block
parameters.description: Split into `factor` contiguous chunks, each its own memory. Suits sequential access across chunks.

parameters.name: type=cyclic
parameters.description: Interleave elements round-robin across `factor` memories. Suits stride-1 parallel access, which is the common case in a filter or stencil.

parameters.name: factor
parameters.description: Number of partitions for block and cyclic.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Which dimension of a multi-dimensional array to partition; 0 partitions all dimensions.

tools.notes: Completely partitioning a large array explodes the register count and usually fails placement rather than synthesis, so the failure appears late. For big buffers prefer cyclic or block partitioning with a factor matching the parallelism you actually need. The older syntax wrote `complete`/`cyclic`/`block` directly without `type=`; both forms are accepted in current releases.

tools.name: #pragma HLS INTERFACE
tools.description: Define how each top-level function argument becomes an RTL port: a simple wire, a handshake, a FIFO, a BRAM port, an AXI4-Stream, an AXI4 master for external memory, or a register in an AXI4-Lite control map. It is what makes a generated block connectable, and getting it wrong is the usual reason an HLS IP will not wire up in a block design.

parameters.name: mode=s_axilite
parameters.description: Map a scalar argument, or the function's start/done control, into an AXI4-Lite register map. `port=return` covers the block-level handshake.

parameters.name: mode=m_axi
parameters.description: Make a pointer argument an AXI4 master that reads and writes external memory. `offset=slave` puts the base address in the s_axilite map.

parameters.name: mode=axis
parameters.description: AXI4-Stream port, for streaming data between kernels or to a DMA.

parameters.name: mode=ap_none | ap_vld | ap_ack | ap_hs | ap_fifo | ap_memory | bram
parameters.description: The simpler block-level protocols: a bare wire, a valid or handshake pair, a FIFO, or a memory interface.

parameters.name: bundle
parameters.description: Group several ports onto one physical interface, which is how multiple arguments share a single AXI master or a single control register map.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: Expected transfer size, used by co-simulation to size its testbench memory.

tools.notes: Bundling two heavily used pointers onto one AXI master halves the available bandwidth because they contend for the same port; give independent streams their own bundle. `depth` only affects co-simulation, not hardware, but an incorrect value makes co-simulation hang or read past the end of its buffer.

tools.name: #pragma HLS DATAFLOW
tools.description: Let the functions or loops in a region run concurrently as a pipeline of tasks connected by channels, instead of executing one after another. It is the task-level parallelism directive and is what turns a read-compute-write sequence into three overlapping stages, often giving a far larger speedup than instruction-level pipelining alone.

parameters.name: Placement
parameters.description: At the top of a function or region whose statements should run as concurrent tasks.

parameters.name: Channel types
parameters.description: Stages communicate through hls::stream FIFOs or through ping-pong buffers that HLS infers for arrays.

parameters.name: #pragma HLS stream depth
parameters.description: Depth of an hls::stream channel. Too shallow and the stages stall on each other; too deep wastes BRAM.

parameters.name: disable_start_propagation
parameters.description: Stop the start signal propagating through the task chain, used in some streaming control arrangements.

parameters.name: Coding rules
parameters.description: Each variable passed between stages must be produced by exactly one task and consumed by exactly one; feedback, conditional execution of tasks and reuse of a variable break the region.

tools.notes: The synthesis report says explicitly when a dataflow region could not be formed and names the violating variable; that message is the whole diagnosis. The most common cause is a value written by one stage and read by two, which must be duplicated into two streams instead.

tools.name: #pragma HLS INLINE
tools.description: Dissolve a function into its callers so its logic can be scheduled and optimised together with the surrounding code, or with `off` keep it as a separate hierarchy block. Inlining removes call overhead and enables cross-function optimisation; keeping a boundary preserves the function in the reports and lets it be shared between callers.

parameters.name: (no argument)
parameters.description: Inline this function into every caller.

parameters.name: off
parameters.description: Prevent inlining, preserving the function as its own RTL hierarchy. Needed for a function that should be shared rather than replicated, and for dataflow stages.

parameters.name: recursive
parameters.description: Inline everything below this function in the call graph, not just one level.

parameters.name: Reporting effect
parameters.description: An inlined function disappears from the synthesis report, which can make a design harder to analyse even when the result is better.

tools.notes: HLS inlines small functions automatically, so the directive matters most in its `off` form - a dataflow stage that gets inlined silently stops being a separate task and the region collapses. Adding `inline off` to each stage is standard defensive practice.

tools.name: #pragma HLS LOOP_TRIPCOUNT
tools.description: Tell the reports the expected minimum, maximum and average number of iterations of a loop whose bound is a run-time variable. It has no effect on the generated hardware at all - it exists purely so latency and throughput estimates are meaningful instead of showing a question mark, which matters when comparing solutions.

parameters.name: min / max
parameters.description: Bounds on the iteration count used for reporting.

parameters.name: avg
parameters.description: Typical iteration count, used for the average-case latency figure.

parameters.name: No hardware effect
parameters.description: The generated RTL is identical with or without this pragma; only the report changes.

parameters.name: When needed
parameters.description: Any loop bounded by a function argument or a data-dependent value.

tools.notes: Because it does not change the hardware, an inaccurate tripcount produces a misleading latency report and nothing worse - but it will silently mislead a solution comparison. Note the loop label (`loop_samples:` here), which is what makes the loop identifiable in the report.

tools.name: #pragma HLS LATENCY
tools.description: Constrain the latency of a function, loop or region to a minimum or maximum number of clock cycles. A maximum forces the scheduler to work harder, spending resources to hit the target; a minimum lets it relax and share resources when finishing early has no value. It is the directive to reach for when an interface has a fixed timing budget.

parameters.name: max
parameters.description: Upper bound on latency in cycles. If it cannot be met, synthesis issues a warning and produces the best it can rather than failing.

parameters.name: min
parameters.description: Lower bound. Telling the scheduler that finishing sooner is worthless lets it share operators and save area.

parameters.name: Scope
parameters.description: Applies to the function, loop or region it is placed in.

parameters.name: Interaction
parameters.description: Combines with PIPELINE and ALLOCATION; an aggressive latency target can defeat resource sharing and inflate area.

tools.notes: An unmet maximum is a warning, not an error, so a build can pass with the constraint violated - check the synthesis report rather than assuming. Use a minimum latency together with ALLOCATION when area, not speed, is the binding constraint.

tools.name: #pragma HLS BIND_STORAGE
tools.description: Choose the hardware a variable or operation is implemented with: which memory type an array becomes (block RAM, UltraRAM, LUT RAM, registers) and how many ports it has, or which core an arithmetic operation uses. The companion ALLOCATION pragma caps how many instances of a function or operator may exist, which is the main area-control directive.
tools.usage:
#pragma HLS bind_storage variable=<name> type=RAM_1P|RAM_2P|RAM_T2P|ROM_1P|ROM_2P|FIFO impl=BRAM|URAM|LUTRAM|SRL|AUTO [latency=<n>]
#pragma HLS bind_op variable=<name> op=mul|add|sub impl=DSP|fabric [latency=<n>]
#pragma HLS allocation instances=<name> limit=<n> function|operation

parameters.name: bind_storage type
parameters.description: Memory structure: single-port RAM, simple dual-port, true dual-port, ROM or FIFO.

parameters.name: bind_storage impl
parameters.description: Physical resource: BRAM, URAM (UltraScale+ only), LUTRAM, SRL or AUTO.

parameters.name: bind_op impl
parameters.description: Implement a multiply or add in a DSP slice or in fabric logic, which is how DSP pressure is traded against LUT usage.

parameters.name: allocation limit
parameters.description: Maximum number of instances of a named function or operator, forcing the scheduler to share one unit across iterations.

parameters.name: allocation function | operation
parameters.description: Whether the limit applies to calls of a named function or to a named operator such as mul.

parameters.name: latency
parameters.description: Pipeline depth of the bound resource, trading frequency against latency.

tools.notes: BIND_STORAGE and BIND_OP replaced the older RESOURCE pragma in 2020.1; RESOURCE still parses in some releases but should not be used in new code. Moving a large buffer to URAM is the standard fix when a design runs out of block RAM on an UltraScale+ part.

tools.name: vitis
tools.description: Launch the Vitis Unified IDE, the environment for embedded software and acceleration projects built on a hardware platform exported from Vivado. From 2023.2 the unified IDE is scripted in Python with `vitis -s`, replacing the XSCT Tcl project commands for new work, while `vitis -classic` still opens the older Eclipse-based environment.

parameters.name: -w
parameters.description: Workspace directory holding platforms, domains and application components.

parameters.name: -s
parameters.description: Run a Python build script headlessly in the unified IDE's interpreter. The standard CI entry point from 2023.2 onwards.

parameters.name: --classic
parameters.description: Open the classic Eclipse-based Vitis IDE, which pairs with the XSCT Tcl commands.

parameters.name: Platform input
parameters.description: A platform is created from the .xsa written by write_hw_platform in Vivado.

tools.example:
# build.py - Vitis Unified IDE Python API
import vitis
client = vitis.create_client()
client.set_workspace(path="./ws")

platform = client.create_platform_component(
    name="zcu104_pfm", hw_design="./system.xsa",
    os="standalone", cpu="psu_cortexa53_0")
platform.build()

app = client.create_app_component(
    name="hello", platform=platform.get_platform_path(),
    domain="standalone_psu_cortexa53_0")
app.build(target="all")

# Shell
# vitis -s build.py
tools.notes: The Python API and the classic XSCT Tcl flow are separate and not interchangeable; a project created in one is not managed by the other. Check which your installed release defaults to before committing a build script, because the migration landed in 2023.2.

tools.name: v++
tools.description: The Vitis compiler for acceleration kernels. It runs in two passes: -c compiles a kernel source or an HLS .xo into a kernel object, and -l links one or more objects against a platform into an .xclbin that the host application loads at run time. The build target selects software emulation, hardware emulation or real hardware.

parameters.name: -c / -l
parameters.description: Compile a kernel to a .xo, or link .xo objects into an .xclbin.

parameters.name: -t
parameters.description: Build target: sw_emu (fast functional emulation), hw_emu (RTL emulation, accurate but slow), hw (real bitstream, takes hours).

parameters.name: --platform
parameters.description: The target acceleration platform .xpfm, e.g. an Alveo card or a custom embedded platform.

parameters.name: -k
parameters.description: Name of the kernel function inside the source file.

parameters.name: --config
parameters.description: A .cfg file carrying connectivity (which kernel port maps to which memory bank), number of compute units, and clock settings. Far more maintainable than long command lines.

parameters.name: -o
parameters.description: Output file: the .xo for a compile, the .xclbin for a link.

tools.example:
# Compile
v++ -c -t hw_emu --platform xilinx_u250_gen3x16_xdma_4_1_202210_1 \
    -k vadd -o vadd.xo vadd.cpp

# Link with a connectivity config
cat > link.cfg <<'EOF'
[connectivity]
nk=vadd:2:vadd_1.vadd_2
sp=vadd_1.a:DDR[0]
sp=vadd_1.b:DDR[1]
sp=vadd_1.c:DDR[0]
EOF

v++ -l -t hw_emu --platform xilinx_u250_gen3x16_xdma_4_1_202210_1 \
    --config link.cfg -o vadd.xclbin vadd.xo
tools.notes: Always get the design working in sw_emu, then hw_emu, before building for hw - a hardware build can take many hours and fails for reasons emulation would have caught in minutes. An .xo produced by `export_design -format xo` in Vitis HLS drops straight into the link step.

tools.name: xsct
tools.description: The Xilinx Software Command-Line Tool: a Tcl shell that talks to hw_server over JTAG for board bring-up, bitstream download, ELF loading and debug, and that also scripts the classic embedded software project flow. It is the scriptable counterpart of the classic Vitis IDE and remains the workhorse for automated board testing.

parameters.name: <script.tcl>
parameters.description: Tcl script to run, then exit.

parameters.name: -interactive
parameters.description: Start an interactive shell rather than running a script.

parameters.name: -eval
parameters.description: Run a single command from the shell command line.

parameters.name: xsdb
parameters.description: The same shell presented as the debugger front end; the command set overlaps almost entirely.

parameters.name: Classic project commands
parameters.description: platform create, domain create, app create and app build script the classic embedded flow; the unified IDE uses the Python API instead.

tools.example:
# build_sw.tcl - classic XSCT project flow
setws ./ws
platform create -name zcu104_pfm -hw ./system.xsa -out ./ws
platform write
domain create -name standalone_a53_0 -os standalone -proc psu_cortexa53_0
platform generate
app create -name hello -platform zcu104_pfm -domain standalone_a53_0 \
           -template "Hello World"
app build -name hello
exit

# Shell
xsct build_sw.tcl
tools.notes: XSCT needs a running hw_server for any JTAG operation; `connect` starts a local one automatically on most installs but a remote board needs `connect -url tcp:<host>:3121`. The classic project commands and the unified IDE Python API manage separate workspaces and must not be mixed.

tools.name: xsdb target and debug commands
tools.description: The JTAG bring-up command set shared by xsct and xsdb: connect to the hardware server, choose a target in the JTAG chain, program the PL, initialise the processing system, download an ELF and run it. This sequence is what an automated board test runs, and it is the fastest route from a fresh bitstream to a running application.
tools.usage:
connect [-url tcp:<host>:3121]
targets
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "ARM*#0"}
fpga -file <design.bit>
loadhw -hw <system.xsa> [-mem-ranges {...}]
rst -processor | -system | -cores
dow [-data] <app.elf> [<addr>]
con | stop | stepi
mrd <addr> [<count>] | mwr <addr> <value>
bpadd -addr <addr> | bplist | bpremove <id>

parameters.name: connect
parameters.description: Attach to hw_server; -url reaches a board on another machine.

parameters.name: targets
parameters.description: List the JTAG chain; `targets -set -filter {...}` selects the one subsequent commands act on. Almost every failure in a bring-up script is a wrong or missing target selection.

parameters.name: fpga -file
parameters.description: Download a bitstream into the PL.

parameters.name: loadhw -hw
parameters.description: Load the .xsa hardware description so the debugger knows the address map; -mem-ranges declares accessible memory.

parameters.name: ps7_init / psu_init
parameters.description: Run the generated PS initialisation for Zynq-7000 and Zynq UltraScale+ respectively, configuring clocks, DDR and MIO before any code runs.

parameters.name: dow / con
parameters.description: Download an ELF to the selected processor and run it; -data downloads a raw data file to an address.

parameters.name: mrd / mwr
parameters.description: Read and write memory or registers, used for peripheral pokes and self-tests.

tools.example:
# Zynq UltraScale+ bring-up
connect -url tcp:127.0.0.1:3121
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "*PS TAP*"}
fpga -file ./top.bit
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "PSU"}
loadhw -hw ./system.xsa -mem-ranges [list {0x80000000 0xbfffffff}]
psu_init
psu_post_config
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "ARM*#0"}
rst -processor
dow ./hello.elf
con

# Read a register to confirm the design is alive
mrd 0xA0000000 4
tools.notes: Target filter strings differ between device families and between releases, so print `targets` once on a new board rather than copying a filter from another project. Skipping psu_init/ps7_init leaves DDR unconfigured, and the application then fails in ways that look like a software bug.

tools.name: bootgen
tools.description: Package a bitstream, first-stage boot loader, platform management firmware, U-Boot and application ELFs into a single bootable image, described by a boot image format (.bif) file. It also handles authentication, encryption and partition placement, and it is the last step before a board can boot standalone from flash or SD.

parameters.name: -arch
parameters.description: Device architecture: zynq (7000), zynqmp (UltraScale+) or versal.

parameters.name: -image
parameters.description: The .bif file listing the partitions, their attributes and their load or entry addresses.

parameters.name: -o
parameters.description: Output image, conventionally BOOT.BIN.

parameters.name: -w on
parameters.description: Overwrite an existing output file rather than erroring.

parameters.name: bif attributes
parameters.description: [bootloader] marks the FSBL, [destination_cpu=...] targets a core, [pmufw_image] and [destination_device=pl] place firmware and the bitstream.

parameters.name: Security attributes
parameters.description: [authentication=rsa], [encryption=aes] and related keys produce a signed or encrypted boot image.

tools.example:
# boot.bif
# the_ROM_image:
# {
#   [bootloader, destination_cpu=a53-0] fsbl.elf
#   [pmufw_image] pmufw.elf
#   [destination_device=pl] top.bit
#   [destination_cpu=a53-0, exception_level=el-2] bl31.elf
#   [destination_cpu=a53-0, exception_level=el-2, load=0x08000000] u-boot.elf
# }

bootgen -arch zynqmp -image boot.bif -o BOOT.BIN -w on -log info

# Then write it to QSPI flash on the board
program_flash -f BOOT.BIN -offset 0 -flash_type qspi-x4-single \
  -fsbl fsbl.elf -cable type xilinx_tcf url TCP:127.0.0.1:3121
tools.notes: Partition order in the .bif matters: the bootloader must come first, and on Zynq UltraScale+ the PMU firmware must precede anything that depends on it. An image that builds cleanly but does not boot is nearly always an ordering or destination_cpu mistake rather than a bootgen failure.

tools.name: program_flash
tools.description: Write a boot image into the configuration flash attached to the device - QSPI, BPI or an SD-backed arrangement - so the board boots standalone without JTAG. It uses a first-stage boot loader running on the target to drive the flash controller, which is why an FSBL must be supplied.

parameters.name: -f
parameters.description: Image file to write, normally the BOOT.BIN produced by bootgen.

parameters.name: -offset
parameters.description: Byte offset in flash. 0 for the primary boot image; a non-zero offset is used for a golden or secondary image.

parameters.name: -flash_type
parameters.description: Flash device and interface, e.g. qspi-x4-single, qspi-x8-dual_parallel, or a BPI variant. It must match the board.

parameters.name: -fsbl
parameters.description: First-stage boot loader downloaded to the target to perform the programming.

parameters.name: -cable
parameters.description: How to reach the board, usually `type xilinx_tcf url TCP:127.0.0.1:3121` through a local hw_server.

parameters.name: -verify / -blank_check / -erase_only
parameters.description: Read back and compare after writing, confirm the device is erased first, or only erase.

tools.example:
bootgen -arch zynqmp -image boot.bif -o BOOT.BIN -w on

program_flash -f BOOT.BIN -offset 0 \
  -flash_type qspi-x4-single \
  -fsbl ./fsbl.elf \
  -cable type xilinx_tcf url TCP:127.0.0.1:3121 \
  -verify
tools.notes: The wrong -flash_type silently programs nothing useful or corrupts the device's layout, and the board then fails to boot with no error from the tool. Check the board's flash part and interface width before the first run, and use -verify on production programming.

tools.name: Flow Navigator
tools.description: The left-hand panel of the Vivado GUI that lays out the whole flow in order - project manager, IP integrator, simulation, RTL analysis, synthesis, implementation and bitstream - and launches each step. Every entry corresponds to a Tcl command echoed to the console, so it doubles as a discovery tool for the scripted equivalent of any button.
tools.usage:
GUI: left panel in Project Mode.
PROJECT MANAGER > Settings, Add Sources, Language Templates, IP Catalog
IP INTEGRATOR > Create/Open/Generate Block Design
SIMULATION > Run Simulation
RTL ANALYSIS > Open Elaborated Design
SYNTHESIS > Run Synthesis, Open Synthesized Design
IMPLEMENTATION > Run Implementation, Open Implemented Design
PROGRAM AND DEBUG > Generate Bitstream, Open Hardware Manager

parameters.name: Settings
parameters.description: Project-wide options: target part, default simulator, synthesis and implementation strategies, IP repository paths, bitstream settings. Each maps to a set_property call.

parameters.name: Run Synthesis / Run Implementation
parameters.description: Equivalent to launch_runs synth_1 / impl_1 with the configured strategy and job count.

parameters.name: Open Synthesized / Implemented Design
parameters.description: Equivalent to open_run, loading the netlist so reports and the device view become available.

parameters.name: Generate Bitstream
parameters.description: Equivalent to launch_runs impl_1 -to_step write_bitstream.

parameters.name: Not available in Non-Project mode
parameters.description: The Flow Navigator only appears when a project is open; a checkpoint opened with open_checkpoint has no runs to drive.

tools.example:
# GUI: Flow Navigator > IMPLEMENTATION > Run Implementation
# Tcl echoed to the console:
launch_runs impl_1 -jobs 8
wait_on_run impl_1

# GUI: Flow Navigator > IMPLEMENTATION > Open Implemented Design
open_run impl_1

# GUI: Flow Navigator > PROGRAM AND DEBUG > Generate Bitstream
launch_runs impl_1 -to_step write_bitstream -jobs 8
tools.notes: Perform an action in the Flow Navigator, then copy the command it echoed into a build script - this is the fastest way to convert an interactive project into a reproducible one. write_project_tcl automates the same conversion for the whole project.

tools.name: Tcl Console and journal
tools.description: The command line inside the Vivado GUI, and the journal file that records every command a session executed. Because each GUI action echoes its Tcl equivalent here and is appended to vivado.jou, the pair forms the authoritative, release-accurate reference for how to script anything the interface can do.
tools.usage:
GUI: Window > Tcl Console (docked at the bottom by default)
Journal file: vivado.jou in the launch directory, renamed with `vivado -journal <file>`
Log file: vivado.log, renamed with `vivado -log <file>`
Type any Tcl command; use `help <command>` and Tab completion.

parameters.name: Command echo
parameters.description: Every GUI action prints the equivalent Tcl command here before executing it.

parameters.name: vivado.jou
parameters.description: A replayable transcript of the session's commands, excluding queries. Copy from it to build a script.

parameters.name: vivado.log
parameters.description: The full message log including warnings and errors, which the journal omits.

parameters.name: Interactive use
parameters.description: The console has the complete command set, so a design opened in the GUI can be queried and modified from here without leaving it.

parameters.name: History
parameters.description: Arrow keys recall previous commands; the console shares the interpreter with any sourced script.

tools.example:
# In the Tcl Console, on an open implemented design:
report_timing_summary -delay_type min_max -max_paths 10 -name timing_gui
puts [get_property SLACK [get_timing_paths -delay_type max]]
highlight_objects -color red [get_cells -of_objects \
  [get_timing_paths -max_paths 1 -delay_type max]]

# Afterwards, read the journal to capture what the GUI did:
#   less vivado.jou
# and paste the relevant commands into build.tcl
tools.notes: The journal records commands but not their results, so it replays actions rather than reproducing a query session. Renaming it per build with -journal keeps parallel jobs from overwriting each other's transcripts.

tools.name: Design Runs and Messages windows
tools.description: The Design Runs window lists every synthesis and implementation run with its strategy, status, progress, timing slack and resource usage, and is where runs are launched, reset and compared. The Messages window collects every message from the flow, grouped by severity and by step, with links that cross-probe to the offending object.
tools.usage:
GUI: Window > Design Runs   |   Window > Messages   |   Window > Reports
Design Runs: right-click a run for Launch Runs, Reset Runs, Delete, Change Run Settings, Make Active.
Messages: filter by Errors, Critical Warnings, Warnings, Info; click a message to jump to the source or object.

parameters.name: Run columns
parameters.description: Name, constraints set, strategy, status, progress, WNS, TNS, WHS, THS, total power and utilisation - the quickest side-by-side comparison of several strategies.

parameters.name: Change Run Settings
parameters.description: Edit the strategy and per-step arguments; equivalent to set_property strategy and STEPS.*.ARGS.* on the run.

parameters.name: Reset Runs
parameters.description: Discard results and return the run to Not Started; equivalent to reset_run.

parameters.name: Message severity
parameters.description: Errors stop the flow, Critical Warnings almost always indicate a real problem, and set_msg_config can promote, demote or suppress a message id.

parameters.name: Reports tab
parameters.description: Lists the reports generated by each run step, opening them without re-running anything.

tools.example:
# GUI equivalents from the Design Runs window
create_run impl_2 -parent_run synth_1 -flow {Vivado Implementation 2024}
set_property strategy Performance_ExplorePostRoutePhysOpt [get_runs impl_2]
launch_runs impl_1 impl_2 -jobs 8
wait_on_run impl_2

# Compare, as the window's columns do
foreach r {impl_1 impl_2} {
  puts [format "%-8s %-8s WNS=%s" $r \
    [get_property STATUS [get_runs $r]] \
    [get_property STATS.WNS [get_runs $r]]]
}

# Promote a warning you care about into an error
set_msg_config -id {Timing 38-282} -new_severity ERROR
tools.notes: Launching several implementation runs with different strategies in parallel and comparing the WNS column is the standard way to close a stubborn design. Use set_msg_config to promote the critical warnings your team treats as failures so a scripted build cannot ignore them.

tools.name: Design views (Elaborated, Synthesized, Implemented)
tools.description: The three stages at which a design can be opened and inspected, each with its own set of windows: Schematic, Netlist, Hierarchy, Device, Package and the report viewers. Elaborated shows the RTL structure before optimisation, Synthesized shows the mapped netlist, and Implemented shows placement and routing on the real device.
tools.usage:
Flow Navigator > RTL ANALYSIS > Open Elaborated Design      (Tcl: synth_design -rtl -name rtl_1)
Flow Navigator > SYNTHESIS > Open Synthesized Design        (Tcl: open_run synth_1)
Flow Navigator > IMPLEMENTATION > Open Implemented Design   (Tcl: open_run impl_1)
Within a view: Window > Schematic, Netlist, Device, Package, Timing, Reports
Layout menu: I/O Planning, Floorplanning, Clock Planning, Debug

parameters.name: Elaborated design
parameters.description: RTL-level schematic before synthesis optimisation. The right place to check that the code infers the structure you intended, and to spot unintended latches.

parameters.name: Synthesized design
parameters.description: The mapped netlist. Where MARK_DEBUG nets are chosen, the Set Up Debug wizard runs, and the first realistic utilisation numbers appear.

parameters.name: Implemented design
parameters.description: Placed and routed. The Device view shows real placement and congestion, and timing reports carry real routing delay.

parameters.name: Schematic view
parameters.description: Cross-probes with the netlist, the source code and timing paths; expanding a failing path here is the fastest way to see what it actually goes through.

parameters.name: Device and Package views
parameters.description: Physical placement, clock regions, routing congestion and pin assignment, with the I/O Planning layout writing PACKAGE_PIN and IOSTANDARD constraints directly.

parameters.name: Language Templates
parameters.description: Window > Language Templates supplies correct RTL and XDC snippets, including the exact syntax for primitives and constraints.

tools.example:
# Open each stage from Tcl and produce the same reports the GUI shows
synth_design -rtl -name rtl_1          ;# elaborated

open_run synth_1
report_utilization -hierarchical -file ./reports/util_synth.rpt
report_cdc -details -file ./reports/cdc.rpt

open_run impl_1
report_timing_summary -delay_type min_max -max_paths 10 -name timing_impl
report_design_analysis -congestion -file ./reports/congestion.rpt
highlight_objects -color red [get_cells -hier -filter {NAME =~ *fifo*}]
tools.notes: Opening the implemented design is memory-hungry on large parts; a headless build should generate reports with -file instead of opening views. The I/O Planning layout is much easier than hand-writing pin constraints, and it writes ordinary set_property commands into the XDC that can then be version controlled.
